## February 29, 1960

Your birthday comes around once every four years. In sixty-six years of life, you have had sixteen of them — the most recent in 2024, the next arriving in 2028. Most people accumulate birthdays the way they accumulate years: evenly, reliably, one per revolution around the sun. Your relationship to your own birthday has always been slightly mathematical, slightly philosophical, and entirely singular. You were born on the day the calendar admits it cannot quite keep up with the Earth.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, a catastrophe was unfolding in Morocco. A shallow earthquake struck the coastal city of Agadir in the early hours of February 29, 1960, while most of the city slept. The tremors lasted roughly fifteen seconds. When they stopped, between twelve and fifteen thousand people were dead and the modern city had been largely flattened. Agadir had been rebuilt in the twentieth century specifically as a prosperous, modern settlement. It was erased in a quarter of a minute. The Moroccan king immediately suspended the traditional mourning period and mobilized the country for rescue and rebuilding — a response that itself became part of Moroccan national identity. The world you arrived in that morning was receiving its own kind of interruption.

**1960 was a year in which power was being tested everywhere, and failing repeatedly.** Four months before your first birthday, on May 1, 1960, an American U-2 spy plane piloted by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over Soviet airspace deep inside Russia. The Eisenhower administration initially claimed it was a weather research aircraft that had strayed off course. The Soviets then produced Powers, alive, along with wreckage of the plane and its surveillance equipment. Eisenhower was forced to admit the United States had been running systematic overflights of Soviet territory for years. The Paris Summit — a scheduled four-power meeting between Eisenhower, Khrushchev, Macmillan, and de Gaulle — collapsed before it began. Khrushchev withdrew, Eisenhower's final year in office was shadowed, and the U-2 incident illustrated something important about the world you were entering: the great powers were conducting a Cold War in which deception was infrastructure, and when the deceptions failed, so did the diplomacy.

**That same summer**, in Rome, the Olympic Games produced two images that stayed in the culture. Cassius Clay — eighteen years old, from Louisville, Kentucky — won the light heavyweight gold medal and returned home a hero, only to be refused service at a Louisville restaurant and throw his medal into the Ohio River in disgust. Seven years later he would refuse induction into the Vietnam draft as Muhammad Ali, having given a name to the contradiction between what America said it stood for and what it did. And Abebe Bikila, an Ethiopian soldier running his first marathon, completed the race barefoot in the dark along the Appian Way — ancient Roman paving stones — in a world-record time. No African runner had won an Olympic marathon before. He crossed the finish line calmly, not appearing to be at his limit, and stood in the lights of Rome having rewritten what the event looked like.

**The political world was also being redrawn.** Three months before your birth, a young senator from Massachusetts had formally announced his candidacy for president. By November 1960, John F. Kennedy had won — narrowly, improbably, in part because he looked better on television than Richard Nixon did, in an election that was itself a demonstration that the medium of television was now inseparable from democratic politics. He was forty-three. The outgoing president had commanded Allied forces in Europe. The incoming president had been a junior Navy officer. The generational transfer had a quality of acceleration: the country was not just changing leaders, it was changing epochs.

---

**What the sixty-six years look like:**

You were born at the tail end of Eisenhower's America — the contained, conformist, prosperously anxious 1950s — and by the time you were old enough to form memories, that world was already dissolving into the 1960s. You were a child during the Cuban Missile Crisis, a schoolchild during Kennedy's assassination, a teenager in 1968. You came of age in the 1970s, which were not the 1950s or the 1960s but a kind of unsatisfying reckoning with both.

The world of your fifties and sixties brought September 11, two long wars, a financial collapse, a pandemic, and the arrival of artificial intelligence as a daily presence. The mobile phone you carry contains more computational power than existed in all of the world's computers combined the year you were born. The Agadir earthquake was documented in newspapers and wire photographs; today an earthquake of that scale would be livestreamed within minutes by survivors.

---

You share your birthday with roughly 5 million people alive today, which sounds like many until you realize it represents one-sixteenth of the normal birthday cohort — a club small enough to notice each other. Your birthday is the calendar's admission of its own imprecision: that the Earth doesn't orbit the sun in a tidy number of days, and the extra quarter-day has to go somewhere.

You arrived in a year when the map of the world, the balance of power, the face of American politics, and the limits of official deception were all being renegotiated simultaneously. It was an unusually crowded year to enter.
